newsitem.title: CHINA: Asian traders wonder whither zinc.
newsitem.headline: Asian traders wonder whither zinc.

text.p: Zinc was the word on the lips of Asian base metals traders on Monday, with many wondering whether the long-vaunted target of $1,400 a tonne had not become a pie in the sky as Chinese metal flows onto the market.
Spot customers were starting to shy away from the metal, having noticed a softening in prices and expecting a correction, traders in Hong Kong and China said.
London Metal Exchange (LME) zinc eased $12 a tonne on Friday to $1,345, with a rise in stocks and overbought technical indicators suggesting a downward correction might be in the offing.
Total LME zinc inventories, at 423,250 tonnes, are around their lowest levels since December 1992.

Traders and analysts have pointed to the flow of Chinese metal, including non-registered special high-grade ingots, onto the market, saying Asia is flush with zinc and customers are now looking for premiums to fall.
Chinese traders who bought at fixed prices from smelters were offering the metal at the LME cash price, and even at a discount, traders said.
"If they bought their metal at $1,250 and they offer it at $1,300, they are still making money and that is all they care about," a trader in Hong Kong said.

Premiums on Western metal were coming down, another trader said, adding he was under pressure to bring his down below $40 a tonne C&F (cost and freight) basis Hong Kong. Copper, meanwhile, was seen consolidating after failing to make a convincing bid to stay above the $2,545 resistance level.
LME copper lost touch with new one-year highs by the end of Friday business, having touched $2,548 in ring afternoon trading, but pulling back to $2,529, a gain of just $1.
Brandeis brokers said in their daily market review copper may try the downside this week, with nearby support seen at $2,520.
Asian traders described lead as dead.
